solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable copy, its numbering matching the numbers printed in it and the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Harvard fresher, girl in rum dance, ungainly number

indicators.note: the word in tells us the girl is placed within the jumbled letters
ungainly means clumsy and out of shape, so the letters of rum and dance are rearranged

parts.note: a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: A Harvard freshman is pictured with a girl at a drunken dance, clumsy among the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ungainly' makes UNDERCMA from the jumbled fodder. 'rum' looks like the drink or an adjective for the dance, but it is fodder; an underclassman is an American term for a student in an early year.
explanation.definitionFit: In American colleges an underclassman is a student in the first or second year, so a Harvard freshman qualifies.

clue.text: A puff or two might make insecure roof ——

definitions.text: A puff or two might make insecure roof ——

indicators.note: insecure means unstable and loose, so the letters of the phrase are shaken up together with those of roof and the blank

explanation.surface: A gust or two of wind could lift a badly fixed roof.
explanation.walkthrough: Composite anagram: the letters of A PUFF OR TWO rearrange into ROOF plus the answer, which fills the blank; the whole clue also defines an upward puff of air.
explanation.definitionFit: An upward current of air is the sort of gust that lifts a poorly fixed roof, as the sentence pictures.

clue.text: Constituent of opium or cocaine inhaled by nostril once? Death mostly follows

indicators.note: follows places the trimmed word after the first part
something inhaled by the nose goes into it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: NARE is an old word for a nostril
C is slang shorthand for cocaine

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: death is the end
the last letter of the word for death is the one dropped

explanation.surface: A drug-taker's warning: snorting coke ends, almost inevitably, in death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' makes EN. 'once' marks the nostril word as archaic; the question mark warns that cocaine is not really in opium.
explanation.definitionFit: Narceine, also spelt narceen, is one of the alkaloids found in opium, so it is a constituent of it.

clue.text: I put in days on eastern garment almost finished, a fourth

indicators.note: put in means the letter is inserted into the word for days

parts.note: dates are days on the calendar

indicators.note: almost finished means the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: a sarong is a wrapped skirt worn in South-East Asia

explanation.surface: Someone sews an oriental garment, the work days from completion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost finished' cuts SARONG to SARON; 'on' simply joins the pieces. In music a fourth is an interval; the Greek-derived name also means a harmony of the four Gospels.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Greek music theory the diatessaron is the interval of a fourth, spanning four notes.

clue.text: Get foot cut from middle of weapon

indicators.note: cut from the middle tells us a letter is removed from inside the weapon word

parts.note: a rifle is a weapon

explanation.surface: An instruction to take a soldier's foot off at the middle of a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing F from RIFLE leaves the verb meaning annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: To get someone, in the informal sense, is to irritate or annoy them, which is what riling does.

clue.text: Casanova's first present for beloved

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: present, as in attending, means here

explanation.surface: Casanova's opening gift to his sweetheart.
explanation.walkthrough: C is Casanova's first letter; HERE means present, in attendance. Chambers lists the word as an old spelling meaning dear.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an obsolete spelling of the French-derived word for dear, so it describes someone beloved.

clue.text: Those coming first in algebra and second in French? I don't believe it (4, two words)

indicators.note: the letters coming first in each of the following words are taken

explanation.surface: A puzzled pupil asks about first place in algebra and second in French, and scoffs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests exam rankings; in fact take the first letters of 'algebra', 'second', 'in' and 'French', skipping the link 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a scornful retort meaning the speaker refuses to believe something, like 'I don't believe it'.

clue.text: Seamy ultras mixed up with core of collusion

indicators.note: mixed up means the letters are jumbled into a new order
the core is the central letter of the word

explanation.surface: Extremists in a seedy alliance, caught up in secret dealings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'core of collusion' gives U, the middle of nine letters; 'mixed up' rearranges ULTRAS with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Seamy literally means having seams, and the adjective here relates to sutures, which are seams.

clue.text: Succeeded, never associated with allurements?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded in genealogies
nary is dialect for never or not one

explanation.surface: A seducer who always succeeded and never had to try.
explanation.walkthrough: Snares are allurements or traps, so the adjective means full of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Snary means tending to entrap, like a snare, and snares are lures or allurements.

clue.text: Rising block, Tories mostly excited about publicity, one likely to win in vote?

definitions.text: one likely to win in vote

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the word reads upward, so its letters are turned round

parts.note: to jam is to block

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go round the next piece
excited means stirred up, so the letters are rearranged
mostly means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written before trimming
air, as in airtime, means publicity

explanation.surface: A political report: Tories, mostly agitated, about publicity as a ballot looms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' makes MAJ, 'mostly' and 'excited' make ORITE, and 'about' sets that round the publicity word. The definition is a French borrowing for a majority-system supporter.
explanation.definitionFit: A French borrowing for a supporter of majority voting systems, the party or candidate expected to gain most votes.

clue.text: King at home brought up odd job for Paddy

indicators.note: in a down clue brought up means the whole run reads upward

parts.note: rex is Latin for king
in means at home

explanation.surface: A king who lived in, raised to take on casual work in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought up' reverses REX + IN as a whole. Paddy signals an Irish word; the answer is Irish slang for a casual job on the side.
explanation.definitionFit: In Ireland a nixer is a spare-time job done for cash, an odd job outside regular work.

clue.text: The governor occupies position in list from which twelve were chosen

definitions.text: list from which twelve were chosen

parts.note: the governor is slang for one's father, pa
to occupy a position, as in being somewhere, is simply to be, so is

explanation.surface: A prison governor takes a place on the roll from which the jury was drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: The twelve are jurors: the word is an old legal term for the panel from which a jury is chosen.
explanation.definitionFit: Pais is the legal term for the country or panel from which jurors are summoned, the list for a jury of twelve.

clue.text: Tamilnadu's devastated, lad swept away — in this?

definitions.text: Tamilnadu's devastated, lad swept away — in this?

indicators.note: devastated means wrecked, so the letters are scrambled, and 'swept away' removes those of lad

explanation.surface: A news report on a coastal Indian state hit by disaster, a boy carried off by the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Take TAMILNADUS, remove L, A, D ('swept away') and rearrange the rest ('devastated'); the whole clue describes the disaster itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The 2004 Indian Ocean wave devastated Tamil Nadu, sweeping people away, which the whole clue describes.

clue.text: Tussle in the south-west? Local service cut, line closed

parts.note: WR stands for Western Region, the railway service local to the south-west of England

indicators.note: closed means the cut word shuts in the line letter

parts.note: to axe is to cut

explanation.surface: A railway complaint: the local service axed and the branch line shut.
explanation.walkthrough: Western Region was the British Rail division serving south-west England, fitting the dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: A south-western dialect verb meaning to wrestle or struggle, which is to tussle.

clue.text: Toast included in tally of expenses chalked up?

indicators.note: included means a word is placed inside another

parts.note: a slate is a running account, originally chalked on a slate in a pub

explanation.surface: A drink raised in the pub, then put on the tab chalked behind the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A pub tab was once chalked on a slate, hence the question mark; the toast itself is Gaelic for 'health'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gaelic drinking salutation meaning health, used as a toast like 'cheers'.

clue.text: Epic hero? King loses first by bog

indicators.note: loses first means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: a raja is an Indian king
by as in multiplication, three by four, is X

explanation.surface: An Indian ruler loses his place beside a marsh, hardly heroic.
explanation.walkthrough: The hero of the Iliad also gives an old slang word for a lavatory, from the pun 'a jakes' in Harington's Metamorphosis of Ajax.
explanation.definitionFit: Ajax is a Greek warrior in Homer's Iliad, an epic; his name was also old slang for a privy.

clue.text: Burnsian songster in avoiding hawk

indicators.note: avoiding means leaving out the named letters from the bird word

parts.note: the merlin is a small falcon or hawk

explanation.surface: A small songbird in a Scottish poem dodging a bird of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: Burnsian points to Scots usage, as in Robert Burns's poems, where merl is the blackbird.
explanation.definitionFit: Merl is a Scots word for the blackbird, used by Burns, a singing bird.

clue.text: Two signs of wealth maybe creating popular outcry?

parts.note: a fur coat shows riches
ore, as in gold or silver deposits, is another mark of wealth

explanation.surface: Displays of riches provoking public anger.
explanation.definitionFit: A furore is an uproar or public outburst, which a popular outcry is.

clue.text: Cistern supplying what school staff serving top table do

definitions.meaning: a tank of water that supplies a system

definitions.text: what school staff serving top table do
definitions.meaning: kitchen staff serving high table feed the headteacher

explanation.surface: A school water tank and the dinner ladies who look after the head.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits into two words: staff serving the top table feed the head.
explanation.definitionFit: A feed tank above a boiler or system, supplying water like a cistern.

clue.text: Children (tinies)? So typical of nanny, isn't led astray

indicators.note: astray means scattered and out of order, so the letters are mixed after the others are removed

explanation.surface: A note on little children and the nanny who keeps them from wandering off.
explanation.walkthrough: Pool CHILDREN and TINIES, take out the letters of ISN'T and LED, and rearrange the rest. The nanny here is a nanny goat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hircine means goatlike, and a nanny is a female goat, so it means typical of one.

clue.text: Either of two Oxbridge colleges acceptable for 'harmless drudge'

parts.note: St John's is a college at both Oxford and Cambridge
on, as in 'that's not on', means acceptable

explanation.surface: Two university colleges suitable for a plodding worker.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson defined a lexicographer in his Dictionary as 'a harmless drudge'; the clue uses that self-description as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson famously described himself, as a dictionary maker, as a harmless drudge.

clue.text: Bearing witness to finest Act II in play

indicators.note: in play means the letters are set moving and rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre review: witness the second act, the best in the production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is part of the fodder, not a link: TO + FINEST + ACT + II are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Testification is the act of testifying, giving evidence, bearing witness.

clue.text: Hall e.g. among number put up, ultra-modern

indicators.note: among means placed inside the other piece
in a down clue put up means the word reads upward

parts.note: ten is a number
Wes Hall is a West Indian fast bowler, an example of the name

explanation.surface: Someone called Hall, among a crowd put up in a sleek new building.
explanation.walkthrough: Wes Hall was a famous West Indies cricketer. 'put up' reverses TEN to NET.
explanation.definitionFit: Newest means most recent, the very latest, which is ultra-modern.

clue.text: Quaker? Not unlike one he reveres endlessly?

parts.note: as, in comparisons, means like or similar to

indicators.note: endlessly means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania, was a Quaker revered by Friends

explanation.surface: A member of the Society of Friends compared with the man he looks up to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quaker' suggests the religious sect, which also leads to Penn, but the definition is a tree that quakes, its leaves trembling.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is the trembling poplar, whose leaves shake in a breeze, so it quakes.

clue.text: It's for lifting potatoes one planted in trench

indicators.note: planted in means set inside the next word

parts.note: a grip is a small ditch or trench
A means one

explanation.surface: A gardening tip: lift the potatoes after one is set in the trench.
explanation.walkthrough: A graip is a Scots dung fork, also used for digging potatoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A graip is a broad-pronged fork used on farms, including for lifting potatoes from the ground.

clue.text: Strip clubs: reluctant entering French one, being female

indicators.note: entering means going inside the next word

parts.note: une is the feminine form of one in French
C is the card abbreviation for clubs
loth means unwilling or reluctant

explanation.surface: Seedy strip clubs, and a reluctant Frenchwoman going in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strip clubs' reads as one phrase but 'Strip' is the definition and 'clubs' gives C.
explanation.definitionFit: To strip someone is to remove their clothes, to take off their garments.

clue.text: Bacteria? Opening of cut on back of head put off

indicators.note: the opening is the first letter of the word
off means the named letters are removed

parts.note: the occiput is the back of the head

explanation.surface: A medical warning: a cut on the back of the head can lead to infection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put off' removes PUT from OCCIPUT, leaving OCCI; C comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocci are spherical bacteria, the plural of coccus.

clue.text: Group of senior ministers, excluding Rudd, rigidly formal

indicators.note: excluding means the named piece is left out

parts.note: a Star Chamber is a committee of senior cabinet ministers who settle spending disputes
Amber Rudd is a former UK Conservative cabinet minister

explanation.surface: A stiff cabinet committee meets without Rudd.
explanation.walkthrough: Star Chamber is a British name for a committee of senior ministers; Amber Rudd is a former British Home Secretary.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch is used as an adjective for stiff and prim, rigidly formal in manner.

clue.text: One looks out for catch making appearance before end of patter

parts.note: hue means colour or appearance

indicators.note: end of means the last letter is taken

explanation.surface: A con artist looks for a mark, putting on a front before ending his spiel.
explanation.walkthrough: A huer was a lookout on Cornish cliffs who spotted shoals of pilchards and alerted the boats.
explanation.definitionFit: A huer watches from the shore for shoals of fish, the catch, and signals the fishermen.

clue.text: Swell? Crescendo may proceed so

parts.note: to proceed to somewhere is to head towards it, so the word here is to
a crescendo builds up to ff, the notation for fortissimo, very loud

explanation.surface: A piece of music that swells, its crescendo rising steadily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' as a noun is an upper-class dandy, not a musical swell; 'may' only links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A toff is a well-dressed upper-class person, which is one sense of swell.

clue.text: Waterfall, one leaving depression

indicators.note: leaving means the named letter goes out of the word

parts.note: a fossa is an anatomical depression or hollow
A means one

explanation.surface: A cascade falls into a hollow, one person leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Foss, or force, is a northern English word for a waterfall.

clue.text: Short article is apt read? Edits this possibly

indicators.note: possibly means the letters may be rearranged, together with this answer, to make the other words

explanation.surface: A brief newspaper piece is a fitting read; an editor might trim this.
explanation.walkthrough: Composite anagram: the letters of IS APT READ rearrange to EDITS plus the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Para is short for paragraph, a brief section or article of text.

clue.text: Ordinary short sword back round middle of waist

indicators.note: round means the sword word goes around the next piece
back means the word is read in reverse

parts.note: an estoc is a short sword

indicators.note: middle of takes the central letter of the word

explanation.surface: A plain short blade worn back to front at the waist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordinary' is not 'plain': in heraldry an ordinary is a simple charge, and a cotise is a narrow band. 'back' reverses ESTOC to COTSE, and I goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the cotise is a diminutive of the bend, one of the simple charges called ordinaries.

clue.text: English vessel with nothing aboard, one conveying Boney to St Helena?

definitions.text: one conveying Boney to St Helena?

indicators.note: aboard means put inside the ship word

parts.note: a liner is a ship
O is zero or nothing

explanation.surface: An English ship carrying nothing, which takes Napoleon to exile.
explanation.walkthrough: Boney is Napoleon, exiled to St Helena; an eloiner is one who carries something far off.
explanation.definitionFit: To eloin is to remove to a distance, so whoever took Napoleon to remote St Helena was one.

clue.text: Those in the oldest profession, they say, dull as it sounds

definitions.text: Those in the oldest profession, they say

indicators.note: as it sounds tells us the word is said aloud and spelt another way

parts.note: prose as an adjective means prosaic or dull

explanation.surface: Prostitutes, it is said, find the work duller than it looks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The oldest profession' is a euphemism for prostitution, and pros is a slang word for prostitutes.
explanation.definitionFit: Pro is short for prostitute, so the plural names those in prostitution, the oldest profession.

clue.text: Tennis Repton's adapted, relatively safe environmentally

indicators.note: adapted means changed in form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the S of the possessive counts as a letter here

explanation.surface: Tennis at Repton, a public school, has been changed to be greener.
explanation.walkthrough: Repton is an English private boarding school. The S of 'Repton's' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonpersistent chemical breaks down quickly in the environment, so it is relatively safe.
